Total Cost, Not Monthly Payment

Comparing borrowing on the monthly figure is one of the most expensive habits in personal finance. Here's what to compare instead.

Every credit advert in Britain leads with the monthly payment. There's a reason for that, and it isn't your convenience.

The monthly payment is the one number that can be made to look better without anything actually improving. Stretch the term, and it falls. Nothing about the debt has got cheaper — you've simply agreed to pay for longer, and therefore to pay more.

The demonstration

Take any loan and put it into the repayment calculator twice: once over three years, once over seven. Then compare the two figures the calculator gives you.

  • The monthly payment falls substantially on the longer term. This is what the advert shows you.
  • The total cost of credit rises substantially. This is what you actually pay.

Same amount borrowed. Same interest rate. Two very different prices. The only thing that changed was time, and time is what interest is charged for.

The number to compare, and the one to ignore

Compare total repayable. The amount borrowed, plus every pound of interest and fee, across the whole agreement. It's the only figure that can't be flattered by restructuring.

Use APR to compare two loans of the same term and amount, which is what it was designed for. It's a rate, so it can't see term length — two loans with identical APRs can cost wildly different amounts if one runs twice as long. APR is a good tool, most of the time being used for the wrong job.

For mortgages the equivalent figure is APRC, which folds in fees and assumes you stay for the full term. Since almost nobody stays on the same mortgage product for twenty-five years, APRC isn't much use for choosing between fixed deals. What you want there is the total cost over the fixed period, which is exactly what the fee analyser computes, and it's why a market-leading rate with a large product fee frequently loses out to a slightly worse rate with no fee.

Representative APR: what "representative" means

An advertised "representative APR" has to be the rate offered to at least 51% of people accepted. Read that carefully: up to 49% of accepted applicants can be paying more, and the advertised figure is still lawful.

Which means the rate in the advert isn't an offer, and your actual quote may be worse for reasons you never get to see. Get the real figure before you compare anything.

Where the cost hides that no rate can show you

  • Product and arrangement fees. A £999 mortgage product fee on a two-year fix works out at roughly £42 a month of real cost that the rate doesn't mention.
  • Interest charged on fees. Add a fee to the loan instead of paying it upfront, and you'll pay interest on it for the full term.
  • Balloon payments. PCP car finance keeps the monthly figure low by pushing a large lump sum to the end. The monthly payment isn't the price of the car — see PCP against HP.
  • Early repayment charges. The cost of changing your mind, which you only discover you needed once you needed it.
  • Settlement interest. Clearing a loan early can attract up to 58 days' additional interest under the early settlement rules.
  • Insurance sold alongside. Priced monthly, presented as small, and occasionally optional in ways that aren't made obvious.

Paying monthly for things that aren't loans

Two everyday cases where you're borrowing without anyone telling you that's what's happening:

Car insurance paid monthly. This is credit. The insurer runs a check and charges interest for spreading an annual premium across the year. Paying annually is routinely ten to twenty per cent cheaper for exactly that reason, and it's one of the largest savings available from a single decision.

Buy now, pay later. Whether it's interest-bearing or not, these are credit agreements. Several are reported to credit reference agencies, and a mortgage lender who sees a cluster of them reads it as a signal about how you manage money, regardless of whether you paid on time.

The habit worth building

Before agreeing to any credit, get hold of one figure: the total you'll have handed over by the end. Not the monthly payment. Not the rate.

Then decide whether the thing is worth that. Very often it is. Sometimes the number's startling enough to change your mind, and those are the occasions that pay for the habit many times over.
